notes: Double‑declining: multiplier = 2. Straight‑line rate = 1 / useful life.
formulaCard.title: Declining‑Balance Rate

explanation: The [[kw:declining‑balance method]] is an accelerated depreciation method that records higher depreciation expense in the early years of an asset's life and lower expense in later years.
It applies a constant rate to the asset's declining book value each year.
Common rates are double the straight‑line rate ([[kw:double‑declining‑balance]]) or 150% declining balance.
Formula: $$\text{Annual Depreciation} = \text{Book Value at Beginning of Year} \times \text{Declining Rate}$$.
[[imp:Residual value is not subtracted initially, but depreciation stops when book value reaches residual value.]]

teacherCues: Ask: 'Why might a company want to take more depreciation in the early years of an asset's life?'
Explain that accelerated methods reduce taxes sooner.

examples.title: A – Find the declining rate
steps: Straight‑line rate = 1/5 = 20%.
Double‑declining rate = 2 × 20% = 40%.
examples.prompt: An asset has a 5‑year life. What is the double‑declining‑balance rate?

examples.peerPrompt: Think about tax benefits and asset productivity.
steps: Higher early depreciation reduces taxable income, lowering taxes in the near term.
Often, assets are more productive and generate more revenue when new.
Matching higher expense with higher early revenue can be more accurate.
examples.title: B – Why accelerate?

examples.title: C – First‑year DDB depreciation
steps: DDB rate = 2/5 = 40%.

blocks.title: 2. Double‑Declining‑Balance Schedule

examples.title: A – Build year 2
examples.prompt: Cost $8,000, 4‑year life, no residual. DDB rate = 50%. Year 1 depreciation = $4,000, ending book value $4,000. Find year 2 depreciation and ending book value.
steps: Year 2 depreciation = $4,000 × 0.50 = $2,000.
Ending book value = $4,000 – $2,000 = $2,000.

examples.prompt: Explain why the depreciation expense decreases each year under DDB.
examples.title: B – Why does expense decline?
steps: The expense is calculated on the book value, which gets smaller each year.
Even though the rate stays the same, the declining base causes the expense to decline.
This is what makes it an accelerated method.

examples.prompt: An asset cost $15,000, residual $3,000, 5‑year life, DDB rate 40%. After year 4, book value is $3,240. Year 5 depreciation should be?
examples.title: C – Final year adjustment
steps: Normally 40% of $3,240 = $1,296, which would drop book value below $3,000.
Must limit depreciation to $240 ($3,240 – $3,000) to keep book value at residual.
Year 5 expense = $240.

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{DDB Rate} = \frac{2}{\text{Useful Life}}$$ $$\text{Annual Depreciation} = \text{Beginning Book Value} \times \text{DDB Rate}$$ $$\text{Ending Book Value} = \text{Beginning Book Value} - \text{Depreciation}$$
formulaCard.title: DDB Schedule Formulas
notes: If the calculated depreciation would bring book value below residual, adjust to keep book value = residual.
Total depreciation over life = Cost – Residual.

explanation: To build a [[kw:double‑declining‑balance schedule]]:
1. Calculate the DDB rate = 2 / Useful life.
2. For each year, depreciation expense = Beginning book value × DDB rate.
3. Accumulated depreciation = sum of expenses to date.
4. Book value at end of year = Beginning book value – Depreciation expense.
In the final year(s), depreciation is adjusted so that book value does not fall below residual value.
[[imp:Do not depreciate below residual value; the last year's expense may be a plug figure.]]

questions.prompt: Companies switch from DDB to straight‑line when straight‑line depreciation is ___ than DDB.
hints: If SL gives a larger deduction.

questions.prompt: Remaining book value $5,000, residual $0, 2 years left. Straight‑line depreciation per year? (number only, no $)
If DDB in year 4 is $1,200 and straight‑line is $1,500, should the company switch? (yes or no)

visuals.caption: In year 4, straight‑line ($1,080) exceeds DDB ($864), so the company switches.
visuals.title: Switch Decision: $10,000, 5‑year, DDB vs. Straight‑Line

explanation: Under [[kw:modified accelerated cost recovery system (MACRS)]], the half‑year convention is used, but in financial accounting, companies can switch from DDB to straight‑line when it results in higher depreciation.
To determine if a switch is beneficial, compare the DDB expense to the straight‑line expense on the remaining book value over the remaining life.
If straight‑line is larger, switch; the switch is permanent for the remaining life.
This ensures the asset is fully depreciated by the end of its life.
[[imp:The switch is made in the year when straight‑line depreciation on the remaining balance equals or exceeds DDB.]]

notes: Once switched, straight‑line is used for the remaining life.
formulaCard.title: Switch Decision Rule

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: In the year of switch, use the straight‑line amount for that year and all remaining years. [[imp:The switch is not reversible; stick with straight‑line thereafter.]]

discoveryHook.scenario: In year 4 of the computer example, DDB gives only $864 depreciation, while straight‑line on the remaining life would be $1,296 ÷ 2 years = $648? Actually, straight‑line on remaining $2,160 over 2 years = $1,080 per year, which is more than $864. So a company might switch to straight‑line to capture higher depreciation in those later years.

visuals.title: Comparison of Depreciation Methods ($25,000, residual $5,000, 5‑yr life, DDB 40%)

explanation: All depreciation methods allocate the same total depreciable cost over the asset's life; only the timing differs.
Straight‑line: constant expense, simple, widely used.
Units‑of‑production: variable expense, matches usage, best for equipment with uneven use.
Declining‑balance: accelerated, higher early expense, beneficial for tax purposes.
[[imp:Choose the method that most closely reflects the asset's pattern of economic benefits.]]

discoveryHook.scenario: A company acquires equipment for $50,000 with a 10‑year life and $5,000 residual value. They plan to use DDB. Use the blueprint to determine the first three years' depreciation and check when, if ever, to switch to straight‑line.

explanation: Apply the blueprint to declining‑balance problems:
1. Understand: identify asset cost, residual value, useful life, and the declining rate (150% or 200%).

2. Solve: compute the DDB rate; for each year, calculate expense = beginning book value × rate; check if book value would fall below residual; if so, cap the expense. Determine if a switch to straight‑line would be beneficial in any year.
3. Conclude: verify that total depreciation = depreciable cost; book value ends at residual.
This structured approach prevents the common error of ignoring the residual value cap.

notes: If the formula gives depreciation that would drop book value below residual, limit it.
